summary: Specifies the C language bindings for version 2, update 1 of the Generic Security Service API, which RFC 2743 describes at a conceptual level. It tells C programmers exact function and type names to use. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

eli5.summary: The idea book for a security tool was already written. This is the version written out for the C programming language.

questions: how to use gss-api in c
what is a gss-api security context
subtitle: The exact C functions, types and status codes programmers use to call the Generic Security Service API.

tldr.problem: RFC 2743 describes GSS-API only in language-independent terms, so C programmers had no agreed function names, data types or constants to code against.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2744 defines the C bindings: the routine names and signatures, the buffer, OID, name, credential and context types, the packed 32-bit status code, and a header file (gssapi.h) that implementations are to include.
tldr.outcome: Applications can call the same routines for credentials, context setup and per-message protection whatever security mechanism sits underneath. It obsoletes RFC 1509 and is itself updated by RFC 5896.

facts.label: Status code fields
facts.value: calling error, routine error, supplementary info

today: RFC 2744 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2000. It obsoletes RFC 1509 and is updated by RFC 5896.

sections.title: The Four Stages of Using GSS-API
sections.content:
The Generic Security Service Application Programming Interface (GSS-API) gives applications security services without tying them to one cryptographic mechanism. A caller can authenticate the application at the other end, delegate rights to it, and protect individual messages for confidentiality and integrity. This RFC covers Version 2, Update 1 as described in RFC 2743, and obsoletes RFC 1509.

Use has four stages. First, the application acquires credentials with which it can prove its identity. Second, two applications establish a joint security context, a pair of data structures holding shared state such as cryptographic keys and message sequence numbers. During this step the routines return tokens, opaque data that the caller must carry to the peer, which feeds them to a matching routine. Third, per-message services protect application data with gss_get_mic and gss_wrap, and the receiver undoes the protection with gss_verify_mic and gss_unwrap. Fourth, each side deletes the context when the session ends.
sections.eli5: Showing your ID, agreeing on a secret handshake, passing secret notes, then forgetting the handshake when you are done. That is the whole flow.

sections.title: The Routines at a Glance
sections.content:
The routines fall into five tables. Credential management includes gss_acquire_cred, gss_add_cred, gss_inquire_cred and gss_release_cred. Context-level routines include gss_init_sec_context, gss_accept_sec_context, gss_delete_sec_context, gss_context_time and the pair gss_export_sec_context and gss_import_sec_context, which move a context to another process. Per-message routines are the four named above.

Name routines such as gss_import_name, gss_display_name, gss_compare_name, gss_canonicalize_name and gss_export_name convert between printable and internal forms. Miscellaneous routines manage object identifier sets and buffers, and report status as text with gss_display_status. Section 5 of the RFC describes each of them in alphabetical order. Implementations may add mechanism-specific routines, but applications are encouraged to use the generic ones for portability.
sections.eli5: It is a toolbox with drawers: one for ID cards, one for setting up the secret link, one for sealing messages, one for names, and one for odds and ends.

sections.title: Types, Names and Channel Bindings
sections.content:
Integers use OM_uint32, a 32-bit unsigned integer. Strings and opaque data travel in a gss_buffer_desc, a length plus a pointer. The GSS-API routine allocates returned data and the caller frees it with gss_release_buffer. A printable string's length must not count a trailing NUL. Mechanisms and name types are chosen with object identifiers (gss_OID), and sets of them are gss_OID_set. Credentials, contexts and names are opaque handles: gss_cred_id_t, gss_ctx_id_t and gss_name_t.

A name has two forms. The internal form is opaque and may hold names from several namespaces for one entity. A contiguous string form carries one name together with an OID saying which namespace it belongs to. A name that one mechanism has authenticated is a mechanism name (MN), and gss_accept_sec_context always yields one. gss_export_name turns an MN into a form that can be compared directly, for example with memcmp() in a large access control list.

Channel bindings let the two sides tag the communications channel that carries the context. The structure holds initiator and acceptor address types and addresses plus application data. A mechanism computes a MIC over them and binds it to the context token. If the acceptor's bindings differ, gss_accept_sec_context returns GSS_S_BAD_BINDINGS and no context is established. Some mechanisms may include the binding data itself in the token, so confidential data should not be used in channel bindings.
sections.eli5: Everything secret goes into labelled boxes with a length tag. Names are like nicknames that different clubs spell differently, and channel bindings are a note saying which road this conversation travelled on.

sections.title: Status Codes
sections.content:
Every routine returns two values. The function result is a major status (GSS status code). A separate minor_status output carries a mechanism-specific error, and the routine always sets it, even on failure.

The major status is a 32-bit value split into three fields: an 8-bit calling error in bits 31 to 24, an 8-bit routine error in bits 23 to 16, and 16 bits of supplementary information in bits 15 to 0. If the upper 16 bits are non-zero, the call failed. Calling errors cover parameters that could not be read or written or were malformed. Routine errors include GSS_S_BAD_MECH (1), GSS_S_NO_CRED (7), GSS_S_DEFECTIVE_TOKEN (9), GSS_S_CONTEXT_EXPIRED (12) and GSS_S_FAILURE (13), the last being a catch-all whose detail is in the minor status.

Supplementary bits include GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED (bit 0), GSS_S_DUPLICATE_TOKEN, GSS_S_OLD_TOKEN, GSS_S_UNSEQ_TOKEN and GSS_S_GAP_TOKEN. The macros GSS_CALLING_ERROR(), GSS_ROUTINE_ERROR(), GSS_SUPPLEMENTARY_INFO() and GSS_ERROR() pull the fields apart.
sections.eli5: Each answer is a number with three little boxes inside: what you did wrong, what went wrong inside, and extra hints. You open the boxes with helper tools instead of guessing.

sections.title: Optional Services and Flags
sections.content:
The initiator requests optional services by setting flags in req_flags of gss_init_sec_context. The services are delegation, mutual authentication, replay detection, out-of-sequence detection and anonymous authentication, and confidentiality is separately controlled per message by the conf_req_flag of gss_wrap. Both sides learn what the finished context actually offers from the ret_flags output. If a mechanism cannot provide a requested service it proceeds without it, and the application decides whether to abort.

Delegation is the exception: if the application does not ask for it, the implementation must not permit it. When enabled, the acceptor receives a delegated credential handle, which may embody either the original identity A or B acting for A. Some mechanisms force mutual authentication when replay or out-of-sequence detection is requested.

A security context can be handed to a child process with gss_export_sec_context and gss_import_sec_context. The resulting inter-process token may contain keys, so the application must protect it in transit. Support is signalled by GSS_C_TRANS_FLAG. A mechanism may also allow per-message services before establishment completes, signalled by GSS_C_PROT_READY_FLAG.
sections.eli5: When you start a secret chat you can tick boxes, like whether to prove who you are to each other or to hide your name. If the other side cannot do something, it tells you, and you decide whether to carry on.

sections.title: Establishing a Context in a Loop
sections.content:
Context setup may take one or several token exchanges. A portable caller therefore calls gss_init_sec_context or gss_accept_sec_context inside a loop. After each call, if the output token's length is non-zero, the caller sends it to the peer and frees it with gss_release_buffer. If the major status includes GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED, the caller waits for the peer's reply token and calls again. On the first call the context handle is GSS_C_NO_CONTEXT, and later calls reuse the handle returned. On a failure the loop deletes any half-built context with gss_delete_sec_context and stops.

While GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED is returned the context is not complete, and some outputs such as time_rec are undefined. The service flags describe what the implementation expects once establishment succeeds. During establishment, GSS_S_OLD_TOKEN and GSS_S_DUPLICATE_TOKEN are fatal and are paired with GSS_S_FAILURE.

If an application passes GSS_C_NO_CREDENTIAL, it asks to act as a default principal. The RFC recommends an ordered set of rules for picking one, which favors a single eligible principal, then the platform's default network identity, then a mapped local identity, and finally a user-configurable default.
sections.eli5: Setting up the secret link is like passing notes back and forth until both of you say "got it". You keep sending and reading notes until the status says you are done.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points out that using the GSS-API does not by itself provide security services or assurance. Those depend on the underlying mechanisms. Callers must therefore pay attention to the requests they make and to the status values returned, since these state which security characteristics will actually apply.

When interprocess context transfer is used, appropriate local controls should limit access to the inter-process tokens and the sensitive data in them. Appendix A gives the gssapi.h header that C implementations should include, and Appendix B adds constraints for application binary portability.
sections.eli5: A lock-making kit does not make your door safe by itself. You still have to pick a good lock and check that it really closed.

viz.caption: THE FOUR STAGES OF USING GSS-API

items.title: 1. Acquire credentials
items.text: Obtain a handle for the identity the application can prove.

items.title: 2. Establish a context
items.text: Exchange tokens with the peer to create shared security state.

items.title: 3. Protect messages
items.text: Apply gss_get_mic or gss_wrap, then verify or unwrap at the peer.

items.title: 4. Delete the context
items.text: Each side discards its context at the end of the session.
